summary: Ernst Gombrich worked in history, archaeology, and other fields after studying at the University of Vienna. He held positions at the Warburg Institute as a research assistant in 1936 and director from 1959 to 1976, and at the University of London (1956–1959).
An Indologist, Ernst Gustaf Ferdinand Olbers earned his Ph.D. at Lund University (1856–1862). He served as principal at Högre lärarinneseminariet from 1868 to 1879.

Indologist Ernst Haas studied at Berlin under Albrecht Weber, Bonn, and Tübingen under Rudolf von Roth (Ph.D.). He served at the British Museum from 1866 and became Professor of Sanskrit at University College London in 1875, succeeding Julius Eggeling.
Ernst Haeckel studied at Frederick William University Berlin and Humboldt University of Berlin from ~1852 to 1857. He later held an academic post at the University of Jena from ~1861 to 1909.

Ernst Heinrich Meier studied at Jena, Göttingen, and Tübingen under Heinrich Ewald (Ph.D. ~1832–1840). Working in linguistics and Indology, he taught at Tübingen as Privatdozent (1841), associate professor (1848), and ordinary professor (1856), succeeding Ewald.

Working in Sinology and Buddhist studies, Ernst Johann Eitel studied at the Maulbronn and Blaubeuren seminaries and the University of Tübingen (M.A. ~1856–1860, Ph.D. by 1871). In 1898, he became Lecturer in German at the University of Adelaide.

Ernst Kalinka, a scholar of history and archaeology, studied at the University of Vienna (~1884–1889). He subsequently held posts at Chernivtsi University (~1900–1903) and the University of Innsbruck (~1903–1935).

Indologist and linguist Ernst Kuhn studied at Berlin under Albrecht Weber, Tübingen under Rudolf von Roth, and Halle-Wittenberg (Ph.D., habilitation). He taught at Halle (1871), Leipzig (1872–1875), Heidelberg (1875–1877), and Munich as ordinary professor (1877–1917).

Indologist and linguist Ernst Leumann studied in Geneva, Zurich, Berlin, and Leipzig under Ernst Windisch (Ph.D. 1881). He served as professor at the University of Strasbourg (1884–1919) and became an honorary professor at the University of Freiburg in 1919.

Linguist and Indologist Ernst Lewy studied at Leipzig, Munich, Breslau under Alfred Hillebrandt (Ph.D. ~1902–1904), and Berlin under Franz Nikolaus Finck. He held posts at Berlin (1925–1935), the Royal Irish Academy (1939), and University College Dublin (1947).

Ernst Moritz Arndt, working in history and archaeology, studied at the University of Greifswald (~1791–1793) and the University of Jena (~1793–1794). He later held posts at Greifswald (~1800–1811) and the University of Bonn (~1818–1860).

Linguist Ernst Moritz Ludwig Ettmüller studied at the universities of Leipzig (~1823–1826) and Jena (~1826–1828), and studied under Bernhard Hirzel. He held positions at the University of Jena (~1831–1833) and the University of Zurich (~1833–1877).

Ernst Osiander, who worked in Indology and linguistics, studied at the Maulbronn and Blaubeuren seminaries and at the University of Tübingen under Rudolf von Roth (Dr. phil. 1847–1853). He served as Repetent at Maulbronn and Blaubeuren (~1853–1854) and the Tübinger Stift (1857–1860).

Linguist and Indologist Ernst Otto August Heuman earned his fil.kand. at Uppsala University (1877–1880). He worked with the Santal Mission (1886–1898), headed the Church of Sweden Mission (1916), and was made Bishop of the Tamil Evangelical Lutheran Church in 1921.
Ernst Philipp Ludwig Calmberg, active in Indology, studied at the University of Jena (~1828–1830), earning a Lic. theol. He worked as a teacher at the Gelehrtenschule des Johanneums starting in 1819.

Linguist and Indologist Ernst Risch studied at Zurich under Manu Leumann (Ph.D. 1930–1935) and Munich under Ferdinand Sommer. He spent his career at the University of Zurich as Privatdozent (1942), extraordinary professor (1956), and ordinary professor of Indo-European linguistics (1959–1981).

Sinologist and Indologist Ernst Schierlitz studied at Munich under Lucian Scherman (Ph.D. ~1920–1926) and Wilhelm Geiger. He worked at the Bavarian State Library (~1926–1928), as librarian at Fu Jen Catholic University (1930–1938), and as director of the Deutschland-Institut (~1935–1940).

Linguist Ernst Schwarz completed his studies at the German University of Prague (~1914–1920) and the Mittelschulen examination commission. He later held an academic appointment at the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg from ~1946 to 1963.

Ernst Schäfer, active in Tibetology and history/archaeology, studied at Göttingen and Berlin under Erwin Stresemann (Ph.D. 1923–1938). He became a Privatdozent at Munich in 1942 and a curator at the Lower Saxony State Museum from 1960 to 1970.

Working in linguistics, Indology, and religious studies, Ernst Siecke studied at Berlin under Franz Bopp and Albrecht Weber (Ph.D. 1864–1869). He spent his career as a schoolteacher and later professor at the Lessing-Gymnasium (~1871–1912).
